ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Neurology (headache medicine) Referral — Friedrich Nietzsche

code.originalText: Establishing primary care for frequent disabling headaches with nausea and light sensitivity: headache history and red-flag screen, a headache diary, disability and mood screening, the daily combination tablets, MRI and syphilis serology, his eyes and his sleep

text.paragraph: Headache on about 20 days a month with nausea, vomiting and light sensitivity, mostly right-sided, since childhood and more frequent over the past year, with a butalbital combination taken on most headache days, in a 36-year-old writer with high myopia. Please confirm the diagnosis and advise on withdrawal of the tablets and on preventive treatment. [S]
Urgency: Within two weeks, on the day of his two-week primary care review, with the headache diary, the MRI and the eye examination. [S]

list.item: Do his headaches meet ICHD-3 criteria for chronic migraine, and is medication overuse headache present?
Do the MRI, the syphilis serology and the eye findings explain or exclude a secondary cause, given the right-sided pattern, the unequal pupils and his father's illness?
How should the butalbital combination be withdrawn safely, and what acute treatment should replace it?
Which preventive treatment fits a writer with high myopia and constipation?
How should we follow him while he moves between a mountain village in summer and the coast in winter?

text.paragraph: Headaches since about nine, mostly over the right forehead and eye, with light sensitivity, nausea and often vomiting, lasting hours to two days; about 20 headache days a month for at least eight months. No aura. He takes a butalbital 50 mg, acetaminophen 325 mg and caffeine 40 mg combination, prescribed abroad, on about 16 days a month, up to four tablets a day, and ibuprofen on about 4 more. Very high myopia, much worse in the right eye, which has seen poorly for years; the right pupil has been larger than the left since early childhood. Past gonorrhea twice in his twenties. His father died at 35 or 36 after a year of progressive neurological illness whose cause was never established, and he fears a similar illness. No fever, weight loss, neurological symptoms, thunderclap onset, or positional or exertional features. Examination today: blood pressure 118/76; neurological examination normal apart from the unequal pupils, both reactive; no papilledema. MIDAS 74 (grade IV), HIT-6 68, PHQ-9 7 (item 9 scored 0), GAD-7 6, AUDIT-C 1. Ordered today: a 14-day diary, MRI of the brain with and without contrast, treponemal and nontreponemal syphilis serology, and a comprehensive eye examination. Chronic insomnia, without sleeping tablets [S]

list.item: Headaches on most days that stop him reading and writing, despite moving between climates to escape them. [S]
He fears that a brain illness like the one that killed his father may lie behind the headaches. [S]
Very poor sight in the right eye and tired eyes when reading. [S]
Short, broken sleep. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Friedrich Nietzsche was born on October 15, 1844, in Röcken, near Leipzig, where his father was a Lutheran minister. [D]

His father, a Lutheran pastor, died in 1849, when his son was four, after about a year of seizures and progressive neurological deficits; an autopsy described "softening" of the brain. Nietzsche later wrote that his father died "in his six-and-thirtieth year"; medical accounts give his age as 36. The cause was not established. [D]

He had severe myopia, worse in the right eye, and a right pupil larger than the left, both noted in early childhood; at about five an eye examination found that the right eye needed a very strong (six-dioptre) lens. By about 30 the right eye was functionally blind, and in 1878 an ophthalmologist found fluid in the right retina and diagnosed retinitis (central chorioretinitis). [D]

Severe headaches began in his school years; at nine he was already missing school because of them. They were mainly right-sided, frontal and above the eye, came with sensitivity to light and with nausea and vomiting, and grew more severe in adult life. [D]

In 1869, at 24, he was appointed to the chair of classical philology at Basel. Ill health led to sick leave in 1871 and again in 1876 to 1877, and in 1879 he resigned his professorship and received a small pension; he never held another post. [D]

Looking back in 1888, he wrote that in 1879, in his "six-and-thirtieth year," he reached "the lowest point in my vitality," when "my eyes could distinguish nothing that lay three paces away from me"; he resigned at Basel, and the next winter, his "first winter in Genoa," he wrote Dawn "in the midst of the agony of a headache which lasted three days, accompanied by violent nausea." [D]

After resigning he settled into a pattern of spending winters near the Mediterranean, usually in Italy, and summers in Sils Maria. After an unsuccessful spring taking the waters at Recoaro, he went to the Upper Engadine at the beginning of July 1881 and rented a modest room in Sils Maria, hoping the dry, sunny climate would relieve his headaches; he kept a strict daily schedule with five to seven hours of walking, filling notebooks as he went. [D]
By his own admission he had gonorrhea twice in his twenties; whether either infection was in fact syphilis could not have been told apart reliably at the time. [D]

list.item: Frequent disabling headaches on about 20 days a month, with nausea, vomiting and light sensitivity, mostly right-sided, since childhood and more frequent over the past year, with a combination headache tablet containing butalbital taken on about 16 days a month; under evaluation with a headache diary, MRI, syphilis serology and a headache medicine consultation: active, confirmed [S]

High myopia in both eyes, much worse in the right eye, since early childhood, with long-standing poor vision in the right eye and unequal pupils; comprehensive eye examination booked: active, confirmed [S]
Chronic insomnia, with difficulty falling asleep and early waking, worse on headache nights; no sleep medicine at intake: active, confirmed [S]

Diagnosis: a structured headache history, a red-flag screen (SNNOOP10) at every visit, a 14-day diary of headache days, attack features, triggers and every dose of acute medicine, and ICHD-3 criteria; MRI of the brain with and without contrast because the headaches have become more frequent over the past year, are strongly right-sided, and come with long-standing unequal pupils and a very poor right eye; treponemal and nontreponemal syphilis serology because of past gonorrhea, unequal pupils and poor vision. Guideline: Headache Classification Committee of the International Headache Society (IHS). The International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition (2018); The American Headache Society Consensus Statement: Update on integrating new migraine treatments into clinical practice (2021); Choosing wisely in headache medicine: the American Headache Society's list of five things physicians and patients should question (2013); Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines, 2021 (2021) [S]

Medication overuse at intake: explain how frequent combination tablets can keep headaches going; count every tablet and acute-medicine day in the diary; take no more than now and never more than four combination tablets a day until the consultation; no new sedatives or sleeping tablets. Guideline: Headache Classification Committee of the International Headache Society (IHS). The International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition (2018); European Academy of Neurology guideline on the management of medication-overuse headache (2020) [S]

Comprehensive eye examination for high myopia: refraction, pupils, pressure, a dilated fundus examination for myopic degeneration, retinal breaks and lattice, and macular OCT; correction of the large difference between the eyes; the warning signs of retinal detachment and an Amsler grid; dilated examination every year. Guideline: Refractive Errors Preferred Practice Pattern (2023); Posterior Vitreous Detachment, Retinal Breaks, and Lattice Degeneration Preferred Practice Pattern (2025); Comprehensive Adult Medical Eye Evaluation Preferred Practice Pattern (2026) [S]

Sleep: cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia through the clinic's behavioral sleep program, a fixed rising time, a wind-down hour, and no sedative sleeping tablets. Guideline: Behavioral and psychological treatments for chronic insomnia disorder in adults: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline (2021) [S]

Mood: PHQ-9 and GAD-7 at intake and at about two to three months, with direct questions about hopelessness and self-harm at each visit; a safety assessment if a score or answer calls for one. Guideline: CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monograph (2026); Depression and Suicide Risk in Adults: Screening (2023) [S]

Reading, writing and walking: good light, large print and an enlarged screen, breaks every 30 minutes, voice dictation for long passages, sunglasses and a brimmed hat for glare, and his daily walks kept as a protected part of the plan. Guideline: The American Headache Society Consensus Statement: Update on integrating new migraine treatments into clinical practice (2021); Refractive Errors Preferred Practice Pattern (2023) [S]
